Sampling techniques have proven effective in rebalancing imbalanced data. However, existing interpolation-based oversampling methods typically rely on pairwise interpolation, limiting their ability to capture high-order inter-sample relationships, and their inherent smoothing effects tend to suppress high-frequency components, compromising spectral fidelity. Therefore, we propose a Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling method (FH-Sampling) for imbalanced time-series classification. In FH-Sampling, a hypergraph is first constructed in the original time-series space to capture complex high-order inter-sample relationships, and sampling ratios are adaptively assigned to mitigate the impact of noisy samples. The discrete wavelet transform decomposes each sample into frequency components. Guided by the sample hypergraph, FH-Sampling combines high-frequency components from related samples while retaining the target sample's low-frequency component to help preserve important frequency characteristics. Experiments on 24 imbalanced datasets demonstrate the advantages of FH-Sampling for imbalanced time-series classification. We further apply FH-Sampling to aircraft trajectory generation. Experiments on simulated aircraft trajectories show that FH-Sampling produces trajectories that better match the real distribution, highlighting its potential for practical applications.
items.title: FH-Sampling: Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling for Imbalanced Time-Series Classification

items.text: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.
items.title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations

items.text: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices ("clients") while preserving data privacy. However, real-world deployments involve clients that observe continuous data streams from evolving environments while operating under strict resource limitations. Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.
items.title: STORMGUIDE-FL: Stochastic Remote Guidance for Efficient Mining of Federated Streaming Data

items.text: Safety-critical systems such as network protocols and distributed algorithms depend on environmental parameters whose exact values are uncertain. Parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs) model such systems by making transition probabilities symbolic functions of the parameters. For a single quantitative requirement, parametric verification asks which parameter valuations satisfy the requirement. In practice, however, engineers often monitor several safety and performance requirements at once, and one valuation may make several requirements vulnerable simultaneously. In this paper we study multi-property vulnerability discovery under requirement-wise semantics: given a pMDP and M quantitative requirements, we construct candidate regions of the parameter space that may contain violations, and study budgets for random testing under a specified parameter distribution. To solve this, we adopt a two-layered approach in which the scenario-approximation layer provides PAC guarantees on identifying conservative vulnerability regions for each requirement while the testing layer treats random parameter exploration as coverage of overlapping regions and yields a stopping certificate computed from the marginal region masses alone; a composition theorem then bounds the expected non-discovery score by the scenario approximation error plus the testing risk from the two layers. For confirmed discoveries, candidate hits are checked by model checking and budgets use independently certified discovery probabilities. Experiment evaluate these certificates using empirical surrogates and independent confidence bounds.
items.title: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs

items.text: Demosaicing reconstructs a full-colour image from a single-sensor colour-filter-array (CFA) mosaic, where only one colour is measured per pixel. Classical methods make different assumptions about images, from simple averaging to directional edge-aware interpolation, and the directional methods cost markedly more compute. We ask a practical question that a per-image quality ranking does not answer: for a given image, is the expensive directional method worth its cost? Using a controlled simulate-reconstruct pipeline on 80 benchmark images from four public datasets (Kodak, McMaster, BSD100, Urban100), six classical methods, and image-content descriptors fixed before any results were seen, we show that the quality gain of the edge-aware method (Menon 2007) over the best cheap linear method is not constant. It ranges from $-6.6$ to $+6.8$ dB, and on 31% of images it is zero or negative, meaning a cheap method matches or beats the expensive one. The gain is also predictable from content: it correlates with mean image saturation at $r=-0.86$ ($p<10^{-6}$). We then build an interpretable depth-2 decision tree that recommends the best cheap method from image descriptors, beating an always-pick-the-most-common baseline by 20.0 percentage points under leave-one-image-out validation. The analysis uses no deep learning, and every step can be inspected.
items.title: When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing

items.text: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.
items.title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction

items.text: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.
items.title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche

items.text: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.
items.title: Efficient Multi-View Generation with Iterative Global-Local Proxy Attention
items.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Supplementary material is available as an ancillary file

items.text: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
items.title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging

items.text: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.
items.title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions

items.text: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.
items.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
items.comment: 4 pages, 3 tables. Data, code and protocols: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24286137

items.text: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.
items.title: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI

items.text: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.
items.title: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging

items.text: Masked diffusion models sample the tokens of one round independently. Planned decoders first generate a coarse plan, then fill in the tokens in parallel. We ask when a plan saves rounds, how many it saves, and how fine it must be. We study this on broadcast trees: the leaves are the tokens, the internal nodes are the plan, and the edge correlation $θ$ sets how strongly tokens depend on the plan. Errors are measured by the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence $\varepsilon$, and the lower bounds hold for every deterministic value-adaptive rule, also with learned conditionals. We show that a decoder without the plan needs of order $\min\{n,(n/\varepsilon)^α\}$ rounds below the reconstruction threshold, where $α=\log b/(4\log(1/θ))$ rises to $1/2$ at the threshold, and that the exponent stays below $1/2$ above it (binary channel: $0.02\leθ\le0.98$). With the plan, $\log_b n+1$ rounds suffice. In the binary model below the threshold, a plan with units of $m$ tokens needs of order $\log_b(n/m)+\min\{m,(n/\varepsilon)^α\}$ rounds, so it gives logarithmic depth exactly when $m$ is logarithmic. A plan therefore helps most near the threshold, and only if its units are small. Exact divergence computations in the Gaussian model with up to $2^{20}$ leaves confirm these exponents below the threshold.
items.title: The Price of Not Planning: Parallel Sampling Depth Peaks at the Reconstruction Threshold

items.text: In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.
items.title: Learning What the True Labels Would Teach: Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data

items.text: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.
items.title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking

items.text: Upgrading the embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding the corpus. Recent work reuses the old index through adapters or window re-ranking. Across sixteen model pairs on passage and code corpora, plus eleven on Natural Questions (NQ), we find three results. First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.
items.title: When the Bill Falls: Reusing the Old Index Defers,Never Avoids, Re-encoding in Complete Embedding-Model Migration

items.text: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.
items.title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B

items.text: Vision models built on Mamba are often explained through their selective step size Delta, on the assumption that a token the scan does not admit cannot influence the prediction. We test that in a concept bottleneck model for lung-nodule malignancy built on a single gated, bidirectional selective state-space block. The answer becomes an interpretability framework: a guarantee, a procedure that checks it, and a pre-registered audit of what it explains. For a fixed gate pattern, masking the input of the causal convolution of the block and giving closed tokens zero weight at readout makes the concept and task logits exactly invariant to the closed tokens. Gating Delta is neither necessary nor sufficient. On LIDC-IDRI, a path-by-path knockout over 15 cross-validated models agrees with this in every run: the largest logit change is exactly 0 whenever the conditions hold and between 4.1 and 6.7 when they do not. The gated model reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUROC of 0.8425 +/- 0.0085, level with an ungated Mamba bottleneck (0.8428). The guarantee belongs to the masked model, not to the gate as an explanation. Post-hoc rankers, which inherit the guarantee on this model, order tokens better than the gate. Gate maps from a model trained on permuted labels are as close to the real maps as two real-label seeds are to each other. Under retraining, the tokens of the gate carry more task information than random tokens and, on shifted crops, more than central ones, but no more than the tokens chosen by hidden attention. We therefore read the gate as a certified support set produced by mask supervision. Splitting the Oracle Impurity Score into own-concept and cross-concept parts reveals differences the aggregate score misses. Partitioning the readout reduced leakage slightly under an earlier recipe, and the final model sits at, rather than below, the level implied by correlations among the true concepts.
items.title: Certified, Not Explained: Exact Token Erasure in Gated Vision State Space Models

items.text: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.
items.title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control

items.text: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.
items.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering

items.text: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
items.title: Zuse: A Decision Model for European Languages
The Fed Is Worried AI Agents Could Trigger a Bank Run

items.text: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.
items.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction

items.text: Mechanical blueberry harvesting requires a balance between removing ripe fruit and avoiding premature removal of unripe berries that could remain on the bush for a later harvest. However, operators generally lack real-time information about the maturity composition of the fruit being collected. This study develops an event-triggered machine-vision system that measures the maturity of harvested blueberries directly on the harvester. When a filled crate is moved by the machine, an RGB image is automatically captured and analysed using a three-class detector that identifies ripe, semi-ripe, and unripe berries. The system operates locally on the existing CPU-only industrial computer and therefore requires neither continuous image processing nor dedicated GPU hardware. During field testing, 79 crate images containing 48,634 visible blueberries in manually verified reference annotations were evaluated. The vision system estimated an overall ripe-fruit fraction of 90.22%, compared with 90.97% determined manually. Per-image ripe-fruit estimates showed a mean absolute error of 0.935 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of r=0.967. Maturity estimates remained similar between the two sides of the harvester for which the light conditions varied despite poorer absolute counting performance under direct sunlight. All field events were processed within the available 14 s per-side crate interval. The proposed approach provides a practical means of quantifying one component of harvest selectivity while the machine is operating. Such information could support operator decision-making and, when combined with measurements of fruit recovery and losses, contribute to future feedback-based control of mechanical harvesting.
items.title: Event-Triggered Visual Perception for Real-Time Harvest Outcome Estimation in Mechanical Blueberry Harvesting

items.text: This study proposes a real-time gaze-tracking system that uses a standard RGB webcam to estimate screen coordinates. The system combines ETH-XGaze-based gaze estimation with nine-point calibration and polynomial ridge regression. To reduce errors caused by changes in head position, it also applies a conditional residual correction derived from head and pose features extracted with RTMPose. Whether this correction is used depends on the reliability of the detected features and the characteristics of the calibration data. In a preliminary experiment, one participant completed trials at 12 screen targets. The resulting mean screen-coordinate error was 204.24 pixels, which was 35.83% lower than that of xgaze-js and 57.69% lower than that of gaze_tracker. The system produced valid gaze estimates for all 12 targets. These preliminary findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining user-specific calibration with conditional pose-based correction for webcam gaze tracking. Because the evaluation involved only one participant, further experiments with more participants and a wider range of postures are required.
items.title: A Study on Performance Enhancement of a Webcam-Based Real-Time Eye-Tracking System

items.text: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.
items.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control

items.text: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence
items.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces

items.text: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
items.title: Sparse Attention for Visual Generation: Toward Algorithm-System Co-Design

items.text: Numerical simulations of landslides are commonly used to forecast impact areas. Full physics-based models provide accurate predictions, but their computational expense can preclude their use for large parameter sweeps. To achieve efficient modelling for such cases, we developed a physics-constrained neural network to emulate full landslide runout in a time-discretised manner. This emulator is trained on over 200,000 samples, each consisting of a pair of landslide thicknesses and velocities on a given DEM with a fixed time interval. To constrain the model's physical consistency, we define physics-based loss functions based on mass conservation and the system's kinetic energy loss. The model demonstrates high fidelity across the test dataset, achieving root mean square errors of approximately 0.06 m for thickness and 0.11 m/s for velocity in single-step predictions. In autoregressive rollout, these errors evolved modestly to about 0.21 m and 0.09 m/s after 110 iterations, while greatly improving computational efficiency by more than 50 times.
items.title: A physics-constrained emulator for time-discretised landslide runout modelling

items.text: A composite score can rank AI use cases while leaving the permitted operating scope and the evidence required for expansion unspecified. We treat the unit of decision as a use case at a proposed scope (authority, human mediation, limits, volume, environment, population) and define three decisions: screen the scope, fund the experiment, and authorize expansion only when residual risk is acceptable and evidence of incremental net value applies at that scope. A risk track (R1-R4) is implemented as an explicit decision table with vetoes and documented precedence, and a value track follows four evidence stages with each transition needing its own evidence. Funding uses expected value of perfect information as an upper bound and the value of sample information for the specific experiment. A quantified expected-loss check, required where policy says so, computes the containment an expansion needs and credits a control only on evidence measured at the proposed scope; in a synthetic scenario the highest-value control design fails that test while a smaller scope passes. A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation and knowledge-assistant use cases, including a synthetic matched-scope fixture and a transferability stress test (value evidence is simulated, not realized), and compares it with a public AWS sample. Thresholds and appetite are prototype policy requiring field validation.
items.title: Which AI Use Cases Deserve a Pilot? A Risk and Value Framework for Funding, Scoping, and Scaling AI
items.comment: 18 pages. All results use synthetic data. A companion Python package reproduces the tables

items.text: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.
items.title: Expertise capture in workplace AI

items.text: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.
items.title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
items.comment: Comment on arXiv:2407.21407 ("Deep Fréchet Regression"). This discussion comment will appear in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA)

items.text: Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks. We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference. We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.
items.title: TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases

items.text: Many materials and tissues, including carbon-nanotube sheets, collagen and paper, comprise overlapping strands whose arrangement influences their effective properties. Measuring this geometry from micrographs requires individual strands to be traced through crossings and signal gaps, which merge distinct strands or split one strand into disconnected fragments. We present PLECTA (from Latin plecta, a braid), a deterministic method that segments individual strands using only a binary image whose foreground pixels mark strand centrelines. At each junction, PLECTA selects which strand segments continue into one another while allowing segments to terminate. It formulates this decision as an exact maximum-weight partial-matching problem, with an explicit penalty for unpaired segments and no restriction on the number of segments entering a junction. The output permits crossing pixels to belong to multiple strands. On synthetic scenes, PLECTA resolved strand identities more accurately than three released alternatives at every density tested. The same ranking held on an independently published generator run at its own settings. A separate stage uses the corresponding greyscale micrograph to estimate which strand lies on top at each crossing. The complete workflow is demonstrated on scanning electron micrographs of carbon nanotube sheets, from raw images to individual strand instances with estimated crossing order, without manual annotations for training or as pipeline inputs.
items.title: PLECTA: Overlap-aware instance segmentation of dense strand networks from binary masks

items.text: Recent inversion-free, flow-based image editing methods evolve the source image toward the target via a differential velocity field. We observe that this velocity field does not explicitly account for which regions should be preserved, leading to unintended drift in non-editing regions. To address this, we formulate source fidelity control as a stochastic optimal control problem in which a selective fidelity term on the editing residual is enforced along the editing trajectory. Solving this problem and approximating its solution yields the Residual Gating Principle: each latent component is pulled back toward the source with a gain that decays exponentially with the local residual magnitude, so that small deviations are suppressed while large, semantically meaningful edits pass through unimpeded. The proposed method, RAGE, requires only one lightweight gated interpolation per sampling step, involves no mask estimation, attention maps, retraining, or architecture-specific modifications, and is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors. On PIE-Bench, RAGE achieves the best overall rank among 17 methods and substantially improves background preservation on both Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX backbones while maintaining competitive editing quality.
items.title: RAGE: Residual-Adaptive Gating for Flow-Based Image Editing

items.text: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.
items.title: PlainPairs: A Corpus Pairing the Prescriber and Patient Texts of U.S. Prescription Medicine Labels

items.text: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.
items.title: MetricHand: Geometry-Aware Flow Matching for 4D Hand Reconstruction in Metric World Space

items.text: Automatic sleep staging models are predominantly developed on healthy sleepers and generalize poorly to clinical populations with fragmented sleep. Across three cohorts (patients with stroke, isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder, and other sleep disorders), we observe 2-3x more awakenings per hour, nearly twice as much N1, and less REM sleep than in healthy sleepers. We propose a label-efficient teacher-student framework for wearable-scale sleep staging. SleepGPT (136M parameters), adapted using labels from 25% of training patients, supervises a causal CNN-GRU (31k parameters; 122 KB) that stages EEG, EOG, or both in real time. We introduce Gcv-TAD, a new black-box transition-aware distillation loss. It emphasizes uncommon stage transitions while discounting those that vary across patients, using a prior estimated from labelled patients. In patient-wise 10-fold cross-validation, Gcv-TAD improves per-patient macro F1 over supervised training on the same labels by +3.2 to +7.6 points on average. Gains are largest on N1, and performance approaches full-label training.
items.title: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations

items.text: Music listening is intrinsically tied to emotion, which drifts continuously within a single session. Although modern browsers interface with wearable brain-computer interfaces, recommendation systems remain structured around discrete logs and lack the infrastructure to integrate continuous physiological signals. Furthermore, existing affect-aware models rely on static user profiles and offline training, failing to serve anonymous newcomers without model retraining. We present a web platform that resolves both challenges. Pairing with a consumer electroencephalogram (EEG) headband over Web Bluetooth, the system captures live EEG, mapping frontal alpha asymmetry and arousal index to normalized valence-arousal proxy coordinates on Russell's circumplex plane. Driven by these coordinates, an affective adapter unifies structurally diverse recommendation backbones under a shared live scoring mechanism. By parameterizing anonymous visitors through a few favorite tracks, the module recommends tracks conditioned on live proxy coordinates. This demonstrates that real-time EEG-derived control signals can steer recommendations without persistent user tables or model retraining.
items.title: EE-Motion: An EEG-based Web Architecture for Live Affective Music Recommendation

items.text: We investigate two single--layer neural-network architectures for accelerating four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles in practical use; both transfer directly without retraining. The first is a gauge-covariant parallel transport convolution (PTC) network that directly reduces the number of generalized conjugate residual (GCR) solver iterations. The second is a CNN-like network used together with a multigrid-inspired algorithm. The two approaches can be combined to further reduce GCR iterations. PTC transfers without retraining across lattice volumes, lattice spacings, and pion masses while maintaining comparable acceleration, whereas the CNN-like network transfers directly from small- to large-volume ensembles with strong acceleration. A cost comparison accounting for both basis construction and solves shows that the proposed scheme is more advantageous for large-volume ensembles than for small-volume ones.
items.title: Transferable neural-network preconditioners for Wilson--Clover propagator inversions

items.text: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.
items.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands

items.text: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.
items.title: Joint Learning of Control Lyapunov Functions and Controllers via Stable-by-Design Surrogates

items.text: Causal discovery for continuous-time stochastic processes with latent confounding typically faces a trade-off between (i) approaches that are highly informative about the causal structure but are difficult to test statistically, and (ii) approaches that admit practical tests from data but yield more coarse-grained conclusions, potentially not leveraging the direction of time. We introduce W-separation, an asymmetric graphical criterion for directed mixed graphs defined as a quaternary relation that allows distinct conditioning on past and future components. This added flexibility yields a highly informative graphical independence model while preserving testability. W-separation satisfies a global Markov property for a broad class of stochastic differential equations with latent confounding, linking it to conditional independence relations among coordinate processes that are testable from data. A central result of this work is the full characterization of W-Markov equivalence classes: we show that every equivalence class admits a unique greatest element that serves as a canonical representative and a principled target for learning algorithms. In addition, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which directed or bidirected edges can be added without altering the induced independence model.
items.title: Markov-Equivalent Conditional Independence Graphs on Path Spaces

items.text: The Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system, on the Hopf algebra of non-planar binary forests, that models the action of Merge on workspaces in Chomsky's Minimalist Model of syntax, satisfies a universal property, determined by the fact that the Merge operation is a Hochschild 1-cocycle. This universal property has an interpretation in terms of models of the syntax-semantics interface, as it shows that, if the side of semantics possesses a sufficiently rich compositional structure, then that structure is uniquely induced by the syntactic Merge, once the semantic values of lexical items and syntactic features are assigned. We illustrate how this universality works by showing, in particular, full compatibility of this Hopf algebraic formulation with Heim-Kratzer semantics.
items.title: Hochschild Cocycle and Universality of Merge

items.text: Meetings last up to an hour, and nobody knows in advance how many people will speak. Neural diarizers with a fixed number of output slots, such as Streaming Sortformer and Nemotron-3, are accurate and run online, but they cannot name more speakers than they have slots. We remove this limit without retraining. The slot head keeps deciding who is active and when speech overlaps, and speaker embeddings are clustered inside a single slot, with the official e-means algorithm, only after every slot has been used. In the streaming system, re-clustering is confined to a bounded window, labels are revised for a few seconds, and identities are anchored to the slots of the head. The resulting system has no limit on the number of speakers and stays accurate when speakers outnumber the slots, where fixed-slot models break down. On meetings that grow to an hour it stays far more accurate than Streaming Sortformer, which accumulates errors, and its cost per update does not grow with the meeting. The same recipe turns the four-slot Streaming Sortformer into an open-speaker system. Across recordings, e-means makes it affordable to link the speakers of a large archive frame by frame, a task that arises when conversational corpora are prepared, and it reaches the clustering quality of Lloyd's k-means several times faster. The method needs little tuning, and e-means runs with its default recipe from a few hundred to more than a million embeddings.
items.title: eDIAR: Training-Free Open-Speaker Streaming Diarization for Long Meetings and Large Archives via e-means

items.text: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.
items.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K

items.text: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.
items.title: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories

items.text: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.
items.title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning

items.text: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters minimize instantaneous deviation from a nominal control command, but a sequence of pointwise-minimal interventions need not minimize cumulative intervention effort. This paper proposes a discrete-time non-myopic safety filter using a learned approximation of the optimal intervention cost-to-go over CBF-admissible policies. The approximation enters through a relaxed Bellman-residual constraint, while the original barrier condition remains hard. Feasibility is equivalent to that of the conventional CBF filter, and forward invariance remains independent of approximation accuracy under the stated assumptions. We derive a trajectory-wise performance certificate that requires neither the optimal value function nor an approximation-error bound. Under additional approximation and horizon assumptions, a suboptimality bound contains an explicit endpoint approximation-error term together with accumulated tolerance and relaxation terms. Numerical results for a collision-avoidance problem show an approximately 50% reduction in mean cumulative intervention effort relative to conventional CBF filtering over 100 initial conditions not used during training or parameter selection. The improvement is consistent across three independently trained networks, while maintaining the prescribed safety constraints and requiring less online computation than the tested predictive filter.
items.title: Non-Myopic Safety Filtering with Learned Intervention Cost-to-Go
